extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting to literary agents / aspiring authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing one or more versions of a book synopsis to submit to literary agents, explaining format, length, tense, content (plot/characters/themes), and how the synopsis interacts with the query letter and proposal. Focuses on fiction, memoir, narrative nonfiction, and other nonfiction distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format
rubrics_metrics.description: Always double-space a book synopsis, indent your paragraphs, and don’t include spaces or extra line breaks in between your paragraphs. You should also include the word “Synopsis” at the top of the page, along with the title of your book and your name. Don’t use a cover page. Use Times New Roman font, 12-point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation matters; follow these exact formatting conventions so the synopsis looks professional and consistent with agent expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and multiple versions
rubrics_metrics.description: You’ll need two or three different versions of your book synopsis depending on genre. For fiction, memoir, or narrative nonfiction: short version 1–2 pages (most agents agree); long version can be up to five pages (many agents satisfied), though some agents request one synopsis page per 25–40 manuscript pages. Always submit the short version when an agent asks for one. For other nonfiction: short version should be 1–2 paragraphs and the long version 1–2 pages; include the short version in the query letter and the long version in the book proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create genre-appropriate short and long synopses; follow any agent-specific instructions (they may override the general guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style should match the book
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, write your book synopsis using the same style that you used to write your book or sample chapters. If your book is academic, write an academic synopsis. If your book is humorous, write a humorous book synopsis. If your book is highbrow or literary, write a book synopsis in the same style. Your book, query letter, and book synopses should have a similar style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency of voice between sample chapters, query, and synopsis helps agents judge whether you can deliver the book you describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your book synopsis present tense and in third person—even if your book is written in first person. However, if your book is memoir, your book synopsis should be past tense, first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard present/third-person convention for most books unless genre-specific norms (memoir) require otherwise; this aids readability and agent expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything in your book synopsis should flow together: ideas, sentences, and paragraphs. Make sure you don’t rush this part of the process. Literary agents and publishers will evaluate your book synopsis to help determine whether you’re a professional writer, and whether they should read your book. So give your book synopsis the same careful attention that your book and query letter deserve. Everything matters when you’re trying to get a literary agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the synopsis as a professional writing sample—clear transitions, logical progression, and polished prose matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (what happens)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re writing nonfiction, explain exactly what information or content is in your book and talk about how it’s organized if that’s relevant. If you’re writing fiction, think of your plot as the external events–the action that’s taking place. Include information about important subplots as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover the main arc and important subplots succinctly; for nonfiction be explicit about content and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (primary characters and stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re writing fiction, who are your primary characters? Where do they come from? And what role do they play in the story? What do they want and what are their main conflicts? What’s at stake? Don’t skip these important details–but don’t include too much detail, either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify protagonists and key players, their objectives, conflicts, and the stakes; avoid extraneous backstory or minor characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: There are powerful themes driving your book. What are they? Love? Desire? Forgiveness? If you’re writing fiction your themes, plot, and your main characters are hard to separate. Make sure you reveal what your main characters desire, and why. What’s preventing them from getting what they want–what’s the conflict? And how your main characters are different by the end of the book. If you’re writing nonfiction themes are still important. Don’t just talk about the information or content in your book. Explain why it matters (or should matter) to the reader. What pain or problem will your book solve? What’s the bigger picture?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction note character transformation and thematic through-lines; for nonfiction articulate the book’s purpose, problem solved, and broader relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoilers and revealing the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary agents don’t read books for pleasure. At least, not all the time. And not when they’re at work. So don’t worry about “spoiling” the ending to your book by giving it away in your book synopsis. If literary agents or book publishers don’t want to know what happens at the end of your book, they won’t read your book synopsis until they’re finished reading your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the ending and key resolutions—agents expect to see the full arc in a synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense and opening hook
rubrics_metrics.description: No matter what genre(s) your book fits into, suspense is important. You don’t have to write thrillers to create curiosity and suspense. Begin your book synopsis with a great hook whether you’re writing fiction or nonfiction. Everyone knows that your book has to be interesting for literary agents to read it–so does your book synopsis. Tease literary agents and make them hungry for more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a compelling hook to create curiosity; craft the synopsis to maintain interest even while summarizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple synopsis versions and overlap with query
rubrics_metrics.description: A lot of the authors I coach ask if it’s okay to repeat information in a query letter and book synopsis. Absolutely. Everything you write should stand alone: query letter, book synopses (all versions), and your book. So you’re going to have some overlap, especially between the short “mini-book synopsis” that goes in your query letter and your shortest standalone book synopsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable and expected overlap—ensure each piece can stand alone while remaining consistent; reuse is fine when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mini-synopsis inside the query letter
rubrics_metrics.description: The shortest version of your book synopsis (usually 1–3 paragraphs) will go inside your query letter. In other words, it will be part of the query letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a concise mini-synopsis suitable for the query; for nonfiction the short version should be 1–2 paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction organization and content detail
rubrics_metrics.description: If your book fits into a nonfiction book category that isn’t listed above, explain exactly what information or content is in your book and talk about how it’s organized if that’s relevant. For nonfiction the short synopsis is 1–2 paragraphs and the longer version 1–2 pages; use the long version in a book proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about chapters, structure, key arguments, and the practical value or problem-solving aspect of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent-specific requirements and submission etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agents will require different lengths (e.g., one synopsis page for every 25–40 pages of manuscript). Always submit the short version of your book synopsis to literary agents when they ask for one, unless they specifically ask for the longer version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each agent’s submission guidelines exactly; when in doubt, provide the version they request.
